def: An antimuscarinic drug that blocks acetylcholine receptors in the brain. Used to treat parkinsonism and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms; side effects include dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion and blurred vision.

A life-threatening complication of sickle cell disease with chest pain, fever, cough and new lung infiltrates on imaging. Caused by sickling, infection or fat embolism from infarcted bone marrow in the pulmonary vessels.

Selective failure of red blood cell precursors in the marrow with severe anemia and very low reticulocytes, while white cells and platelets are normal. Associated with thymoma, parvovirus B19 infection and autoimmune disease.
Small spinal motor neurons that supply the intrafusal fibers of muscle spindles. They adjust spindle tension so the spindle stays sensitive to stretch while the muscle contracts.

The large opening at the base of the skull through which the spinal cord joins the medulla. It also transmits the vertebral arteries and spinal accessory nerve roots; tonsillar herniation passes through it.
An abnormally low lymphocyte count in the blood. Seen in HIV infection, steroid use, severe combined immunodeficiency and DiGeorge syndrome.
A toxin of Bordetella pertussis that ADP-ribosylates the Gi protein, raising cAMP. It causes marked lymphocytosis because lymphocytes are blocked from leaving the blood, and impairs glucose control.

Blood cells derived from the common myeloid progenitor in bone marrow: granulocytes, monocytes and macrophages, red cells, megakaryocytes and platelets. Distinguished from lymphoid cells (T, B and NK cells).

The t(9;22) translocation that fuses BCR on chromosome 22 with ABL1 on chromosome 9. The BCR-ABL fusion gives constitutive tyrosine kinase activity, typical of chronic myeloid leukemia and treated with imatinib.
Loss of nerve supply to a muscle or tissue after nerve injury. Denervated muscle shows fasciculations, fibrillations, atrophy and increased acetylcholine receptor sensitivity.

The skeletal muscles of the pharynx used in swallowing: three constrictors plus palatopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus and stylopharyngeus. All are supplied by the vagus nerve except stylopharyngeus, which is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

The potassium-rich fluid filling the membranous labyrinth, including the scala media of the cochlea. Its high potassium sets the electrochemical gradient that drives hair cell depolarization; excess is linked to Meniere disease.

The sensory structure on the basilar membrane of the cochlea containing inner and outer hair cells. Sound-induced vibration bends hair cell stereocilia against the tectorial membrane, converting sound into nerve signals.

Hearing loss from impaired sound transmission through the external or middle ear, such as wax, otitis media or otosclerosis. In the Rinne test bone conduction exceeds air conduction; Weber lateralizes to the affected ear.
Neurons that release gamma-aminobutyric acid, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain. Examples include Purkinje cells, striatal medium spiny neurons and many cortical interneurons.
Forearm rotation that turns the palm upward or forward, with radius and ulna parallel. The biceps brachii and supinator muscle perform it; the foot equivalent is rolling weight onto the outer edge.
A basal ganglia nucleus that excites the globus pallidus internus in the indirect pathway. Lesions cause contralateral hemiballismus; deep brain stimulation of it treats Parkinson disease.
Both pupils constrict less when light shines in the eye with a damaged optic nerve or severe retinal disease than in the healthy eye. Seen on the swinging flashlight test in optic neuritis.
Removal of blood from a vein, either for sampling or as treatment. Therapeutic phlebotomy lowers iron stores in hemochromatosis and red cell mass in polycythemia vera.
Small secreted cytokines that guide leukocyte migration along concentration gradients to sites of infection or inflammation. IL-8 (CXCL8) is the classic neutrophil chemoattractant.

Process by which cells display peptide fragments on MHC molecules for T cell recognition. MHC class I presents intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells; MHC class II presents extracellular peptides to CD4 T cells.
Inability to form new long-term memories after the causative event, with older memories preserved. Classically follows bilateral hippocampal damage, thiamine deficiency or benzodiazepine use.
Inflammation of the meninges caused by a virus, most often an enterovirus. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose and mildly raised protein; it is usually self-limited.

A slowly enlarging collection of blood between dura and arachnoid, from torn bridging veins after minor trauma. Common in the elderly and alcoholics, it presents weeks later with headache and confusion; CT shows a crescent-shaped lesion.

CD4 helper T cells that make IL-17 and IL-22, recruiting neutrophils and defending against extracellular bacteria and fungi. Differentiate under IL-6 and TGF-beta; defects cause hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome.

A microtubule-associated protein of neurons that stabilizes axonal microtubules. Hyperphosphorylated tau aggregates into neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer disease and also accumulates in Pick disease and chronic traumatic encephalopathy.
Inflammation of a salivary gland, usually from duct obstruction or bacterial infection. Staphylococcus aureus is common; presents with a painful, swollen parotid or submandibular gland.
Stone formation in a salivary gland duct, most often the submandibular gland. Causes pain and swelling of the gland during meals.
A double fold of peritoneum that attaches the small intestine to the posterior abdominal wall and carries its blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics.

A collection of pus within the psoas muscle, from spread of vertebral osteomyelitis (including tuberculosis) or abdominal infection such as Crohn disease. Presents with fever, flank or back pain and pain on hip extension.
Acute dilation of the colon beyond 6 cm with systemic toxicity. A complication of ulcerative colitis, C. difficile infection or Crohn colitis, with risk of perforation.
Benign colonic polyps from dysplastic glandular epithelium that can progress to colorectal cancer by the adenoma-carcinoma sequence. Villous histology and larger size carry the highest risk.

An enzyme that cleaves glucuronic acid from conjugated molecules. Beta-glucuronidase in gut bacteria can deconjugate bilirubin, enabling its reabsorption, and a lysosomal form is deficient in Sly syndrome.
Gallstones in the common bile duct. Cause biliary colic and obstructive jaundice with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin; can lead to cholangitis or gallstone pancreatitis.

Dysfunction of structures in the cavernous sinus, with ophthalmoplegia from cranial nerves III, IV and VI, reduced V1 and V2 sensation, and proptosis. Caused by thrombosis, tumor or carotid-cavernous fistula.
Infection of orbital soft tissues behind the orbital septum, usually spreading from the ethmoid sinuses. Causes fever, proptosis, painful eye movements and ophthalmoplegia; an emergency.
RNA viruses that use reverse transcriptase to make DNA copies that integrate into the host genome. HIV and HTLV-1 are the key human examples.
Seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery between them. A neurologic emergency treated first with IV benzodiazepines such as lorazepam.
Disease of the spinal cord itself, from compression, ischemia, inflammation or degeneration. Causes weakness, sensory loss and upper motor neuron signs below the lesion.
A benign, highly vascular tumor, most often in the cerebellum, that may secrete erythropoietin and cause polycythemia. Associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease.
Use of focused laser light to burn tissue, notably the retina. Treats proliferative diabetic retinopathy and retinal tears.

A personality disorder with unstable relationships, self-image and mood, impulsivity, chronic emptiness and self-harm. Characterized by splitting, idealizing then devaluing others; treated with dialectical behavior therapy.
Disorders of repeated failure to resist harmful urges, such as intermittent explosive disorder (disproportionate rage outbursts), kleptomania (stealing items not needed) and pyromania.
A short-acting benzodiazepine used for insomnia. Enhances GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency; can cause anterograde amnesia and next-day effects.
A short- to intermediate-acting benzodiazepine used for panic and anxiety disorders. Potentiates GABA-A receptors; risks are dependence and dangerous withdrawal with seizures.
A major depressive episode beginning within weeks of childbirth, lasting beyond two weeks. More severe and persistent than postpartum blues; treated with antidepressants.
An IV anesthetic that enhances GABA-A receptor activity, with rapid onset and recovery. Causes hypotension and respiratory depression; prolonged infusion can cause propofol infusion syndrome.

A glutamate-gated ion channel permeable to calcium that needs glycine and membrane depolarization to open. Central to synaptic plasticity and long-term potentiation; blocked by ketamine and phencyclidine.

An NMDA receptor antagonist producing dissociative anesthesia. Preserves airway reflexes and raises blood pressure, can cause emergence reactions, and is also used rapidly in treatment-resistant depression.
Systemic inflammatory response from massive cytokine release after immune activation, such as CAR-T therapy. Causes fever, hypotension and organ dysfunction; managed with tocilizumab.
Bacterial toxins that bind MHC class II and T cell receptor beta chains outside the usual antigen groove. They activate huge numbers of T cells and trigger cytokine storm, as in toxic shock syndrome.
A volatile inhaled anesthetic. Rare causes of fulminant hepatitis and malignant hyperthermia.
A potent synthetic mu-opioid agonist, about 100 times as strong as morphine, used in anesthesia and chronic pain. Overdose causes respiratory depression and miosis; reversed by naloxone.
A weak opioid prodrug converted by CYP2D6 to morphine. Used for pain and cough; ultrarapid metabolizers risk toxicity.
Marked fear of situations from which escape might be hard, such as crowds, public transport or open spaces. Often accompanies panic disorder, leading to avoidance of leaving home.
Deliberate feigning or exaggeration of symptoms for an external goal, such as money, drugs or avoiding work. Distinguished from factitious disorder, where the motive is to assume the sick role.

Deliberate production or feigning of illness to assume the sick role, with no external gain. When done to another person, such as a child, it is factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen by proxy).
A synthetic amphetamine derivative that causes release of serotonin, causing euphoria and empathy. Toxicity includes hyperthermia, hyponatremia and serotonin syndrome.
An antidepressant that inhibits serotonin reuptake and partially agonizes 5-HT1A receptors. Side effects include nausea, diarrhea and sexual dysfunction.
A non-ergot dopamine agonist for Parkinson disease and restless legs syndrome. Side effects include sleep attacks, hallucinations and impulse control disorders.

Drugs that interrupt transmission at the neuromuscular junction for paralysis in surgery. Nondepolarizing agents (rocuronium) compete with acetylcholine; depolarizing succinylcholine persistently activates the receptor.

Autosomal recessive UGT1A1 deficiency impairing bilirubin conjugation. Type I (absent enzyme) causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus; type II is milder and responds to phenobarbital.
An iron chelator given parenterally for iron overload and acute iron poisoning. Binds ferric iron to promote its urinary excretion, turning urine reddish.
Needle drainage of fluid from the peritoneal cavity. Used to sample ascites, for example to check for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, or to relieve tense ascites.

Somatic rearrangement of variable, diversity and joining gene segments in developing B and T cells to generate diverse antigen receptors. Requires RAG1 and RAG2 enzymes; defects cause severe combined immunodeficiency.
CD4 T cells expressing CD25 and FOXP3 that suppress immune responses and maintain self-tolerance via IL-10, TGF-beta and CTLA-4. FOXP3 mutation causes IPEX syndrome.
Cysteine proteases that carry out apoptosis. Initiator caspases (8, 9) activate executioner caspases (3, 6, 7), which cleave cellular proteins.
A type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity skin reaction to an allergen such as nickel or poison ivy. Produces itchy, vesicular rash at the contact site 1 to 2 days after re-exposure.
Donor T cells in a transplant attack recipient tissues, classically after bone marrow transplant. Causes rash, diarrhea and jaundice from skin, gut and liver involvement.
Intradermal injection of an antigen to test immune reactivity. Used for immediate allergy testing and delayed-type tuberculin (PPD) testing.
Innate immune receptors that detect conserved microbial structures and damage signals. Toll-like receptors, NOD-like receptors and RIG-I trigger inflammatory cytokine production.

Primary antibody deficiency with low IgG, IgA and IgM and impaired B cell differentiation, usually presenting in adulthood. Causes recurrent sinopulmonary infections, autoimmunity and increased lymphoma risk.
Autoantibodies against nuclear components. A sensitive but not specific screen for systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases.
Inflammation of both the cornea and conjunctiva. Examples include dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and adenovirus infection.
The most common benign bone tumor, an outgrowth capped with cartilage on the metaphysis of long bones. Usually found in adolescents; multiple lesions occur in hereditary multiple exostoses.
Inflammation of the synovial membrane lining a joint, causing pain, swelling and effusion. Seen in rheumatoid arthritis, gout and infectious arthritis.
Cell junctions anchoring basal epithelial cells to the basement membrane through integrins, linking to keratin filaments. Autoantibodies against them cause bullous pemphigoid.
A chronic facial skin condition with persistent redness, telangiectasias, and papules and pustules. Phymatous rosacea causes thickened nose (rhinophyma) and ocular rosacea affects the eyes.
Birth weight above 4000 to 4500 g. Associated with maternal diabetes and increases the risk of shoulder dystocia and birth injury.

A penicillin combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, extending coverage to beta-lactamase-producing bacteria. Used in sinusitis, otitis and bite wounds; can cause diarrhea and cholestatic hepatitis.
A beta-lactamase inhibitor combined with piperacillin to broaden its spectrum. Has little antibacterial action itself.
A narrow-spectrum macrolide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase. Used orally for Clostridioides difficile colitis, with lower relapse than vancomycin.
Pills containing estrogen and progestin that prevent ovulation by suppressing FSH and LH. Increase risk of venous thromboembolism, especially in smokers over 35 and migraine with aura.

Damage to the optic nerve causing visual loss, afferent pupillary defect and a pale or swollen disc. Foster Kennedy syndrome combines optic atrophy in one eye with papilledema in the other, caused by frontal lobe tumor.
The thickest nerve in the body, from L4 to S3, running through the posterior thigh. It divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves; injury weakens hamstrings and all muscles below the knee.
Laboratory tests on serum that detect antibodies or antigens, used for infections and autoimmune disease.
A tyrosine kinase inhibitor that blocks the EGFR. Used for EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer and pancreatic cancer; causes acneiform rash.
The outermost polysaccharide chain of gram-negative lipopolysaccharide. Highly variable among strains, it is the main target of antibodies and serotyping.
Superficial fungal infections of skin, hair and nails by Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton. They cause tinea, such as ringworm and athlete's foot; KOH prep shows hyphae.
Infection of the intraocular fluids, usually after eye surgery or injection, or from bloodstream seeding. Causes pain, vision loss and hypopyon; an emergency.
A mold with septate hyphae branching at acute angles. Causes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma in old cavities and invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients.
An encapsulated yeast found in soil and pigeon droppings. Causes meningitis in HIV patients, shown by India ink capsule halo and mucicarmine staining.
Gram-negative coccobacilli that are often multidrug resistant. A cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia, especially in ventilated patients.
A sexually transmitted infection by Klebsiella granulomatis causing painless, beefy red genital ulcers. Biopsy shows intracellular Donovan bodies.
A gram-negative coccobacillus that causes chancroid, a painful genital ulcer with tender suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy.

A glycylcycline antibiotic that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, with activity against many resistant bacteria such as MRSA and VRE. Causes nausea and, like tetracyclines, tooth discoloration in children.
An acid-fast bacillus that causes leprosy. Grows best in cool tissues like skin and peripheral nerves, causing numbness and skin lesions; cannot be cultured in vitro, and armadillos are a reservoir.
Damage to arteries or veins from trauma. Hard signs include pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, absent pulses and a thrill.
A paramyxovirus causing respiratory infection, the main cause of croup in children with a barking cough and steeple sign on neck x-ray.
Infection by hepatitis D virus, a defective RNA virus requiring hepatitis B surface antigen to replicate. Occurs as coinfection or superinfection with hepatitis B and worsens its course.
The viral enzyme that cleaves gag-pol polyproteins into functional proteins for virion maturation. Target of protease inhibitors such as ritonavir, which end in -navir.
A genus of filarial nematodes transmitted by blood-feeding flies. Onchocerca volvulus causes river blindness.
A filarial roundworm transmitted by Simulium blackflies that causes river blindness. Microfilariae cause itchy skin disease and corneal scarring; treated with ivermectin.
A dog roundworm. Ingested eggs cause visceral larva migrans with eosinophilia, hepatomegaly and ocular larva migrans mimicking retinoblastoma.
A genus of ascarid roundworms of dogs and cats whose larvae wander in human tissue, causing visceral larva migrans.
A filarial nematode transmitted by deer flies (Chrysops) that causes migratory subcutaneous swellings (Calabar swellings) and worms crossing the eye. Treated with diethylcarbamazine.
A nontyphoidal Salmonella serotype causing gastroenteritis, typically from poultry and eggs. Presents with fever, diarrhea and cramps; mild disease usually needs no antibiotics.

Sudden major change in influenza virus surface antigens (HA and NA) through reassortment of RNA segments between strains. Causes pandemics, whereas antigenic drift arises from gradual point mutations and causes seasonal epidemics.
Overuse injury at the tibial tuberosity in active adolescents from repeated quadriceps traction. Causes painful swelling below the knee, relieved by rest.
A childhood illness from human herpesvirus 6 or 7 with several days of high fever, followed by a rose-colored rash when fever resolves. May cause febrile seizures.
The rise in adrenal androgen (DHEA) production in late childhood, preceding puberty. Causes pubic and axillary hair and body odor without gonadal activation.
A polyomavirus that stays latent in kidney tissue. Reactivates in transplant recipients causing nephropathy and ureteral stenosis, and causes hemorrhagic cystitis after bone marrow transplant.
A congenital aortic arch anomaly where vessels encircle and compress the trachea and esophagus. Causes stridor, wheeze and dysphagia in infants; double aortic arch is a common cause.
Autosomal recessive defect in phytanic acid alpha-oxidation in peroxisomes. Causes retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia and ichthyosis, treated with dietary phytanic acid restriction.
Failure to deliver the placenta within 30 minutes after birth. Risks hemorrhage and infection and may result from placenta accreta.
The number and quality of remaining oocytes in the ovaries. Assessed by anti-Mullerian hormone, FSH and antral follicle count; falls with age.
Tear of the tendons of supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor or subscapularis. Supraspinatus is most often torn, causing shoulder pain and weak abduction, with a positive drop arm test.
Disease of the heart valves causing stenosis or regurgitation. Examples include rheumatic mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis and mitral valve prolapse.
Blood in the peritoneal cavity, caused by trauma, ruptured ectopic pregnancy or ruptured aneurysm. Detected by FAST ultrasound.
Thickening of the left ventricle wall from chronic pressure load such as hypertension or aortic stenosis. ECG shows large voltages; leads to diastolic dysfunction.
Spasm of the masseter and other jaw muscles that limits mouth opening. Seen in tetanus, from the toxin, and with dental infection.
Infection by Coxiella burnetii, acquired by inhaling aerosols from livestock, with fever, pneumonia and hepatitis. Can cause culture-negative endocarditis; treated with doxycycline.
A mold with broad, nonseptate hyphae branching at right angles. Causes mucormycosis, notably rhinocerebral infection in ketoacidotic diabetics, with black necrotic tissue.
The embryo at about day 5, with an inner cell mass that becomes the embryo and an outer trophoblast. It implants into the uterine wall around day 6.
A synthetic progestin that suppresses ovulation and thins the endometrium. Used in contraception and to treat abnormal bleeding and endometriosis.
The injectable (every 3 months) progestin contraceptive. Suppresses ovulation, may reduce bone density, and delays fertility return.
Floppy laryngeal cartilage collapsing inward during inhalation. Most common cause of infant stridor, worse when supine, and usually resolves by age 2.
A serotonin-gated ligand ion channel (the only 5-HT receptor not G protein-coupled) involved in vomiting. Blocked by ondansetron.
Receptor for 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin). Most subtypes are G protein-coupled; 5-HT3 is a ligand-gated ion channel.
A neuropeptide of the tachykinin family that mediates pain transmission in sensory neurons and vomiting. Acts on NK1 receptors, blocked by aprepitant.
The nerve network within the gut wall, with the myenteric plexus (motility) and submucosal plexus (secretion and absorption). Absent in Hirschsprung disease.
Symmetric facial hyperpigmentation, seen in pregnancy or with oral contraceptives. Also called chloasma.
A progesterone receptor antagonist used with misoprostol to terminate early pregnancy. Also blocks glucocorticoid receptors.
A short N-terminal amino acid sequence directing a new protein to the endoplasmic reticulum. Cleaved by signal peptidase after translocation.
A peptide growth hormone mainly produced by the liver under growth hormone stimulation. IGF-1 mediates growth hormone's growth-promoting effects and is used to screen for acromegaly.
Hormones made of amino acid chains, stored in vesicles and released on demand. They act on cell-surface receptors, are water soluble and travel unbound in blood.
Cells that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream. Examples include pancreatic islet cells and pituitary cells.
A hormone from the placenta that raises maternal insulin resistance, promoting glucose supply for the fetus. Similar to growth hormone and prolactin.
A cytokine-type receptor that signals through JAK2/STAT. Binding of GH stimulates IGF-1 production; Laron syndrome results from receptor defects.
Anterior pituitary cells that secrete prolactin. Inhibited by dopamine and expand during pregnancy.
Epithelial cells lining thyroid follicles that make thyroglobulin and thyroid hormones. Take up iodide, with TSH as their main stimulus.
The immediate precursor of cortisol. It accumulates in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, producing hypertension and virilization.
The decapeptide produced when renin cleaves angiotensinogen. ACE then converts it to angiotensin II.
Channels formed from connexins connecting the cytoplasm of adjacent cells. Allow electrical coupling, as in cardiac myocytes.
A covalent bond between two sulfur atoms of cysteine residues. Stabilizes protein structure, as in insulin and antibodies.
Membrane network studded with ribosomes that synthesizes secretory and membrane proteins. Abundant in plasma cells and pancreatic acinar cells; appears basophilic.
Uptake of nutrients, water and ions from the gut lumen into blood or lymph, mainly in the small intestine.
Surgical removal of parathyroid tissue. Treats primary hyperparathyroidism; complications include hypocalcemia.
Bone disease from chronic kidney failure caused by phosphate retention, low calcitriol and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Includes osteitis fibrosa cystica and osteomalacia.
Failure of the thyroid gland to form or descend normally. Includes agenesis and ectopic thyroid and is the main cause of congenital hypothyroidism.
An MHC class II allele associated with autoimmune diseases including type 1 diabetes, Graves disease and lupus.
Fibrous tissue replacing retroperitoneal fat, encasing the ureters and aorta. Causes hydronephrosis; associated with IgG4 disease, methysergide.
An irreversible nonselective alpha blocker used before surgery of pheochromocytoma. Causes orthostatic hypotension and reflex tachycardia.
Branch of the abdominal aorta at L3 that supplies the hindgut: descending colon, sigmoid and upper rectum. Marks the watershed area at the splenic flexure.
A hormone made mainly by the liver that stimulates megakaryocyte growth and platelet production through the c-Mpl receptor.
A liver protein that binds testosterone and estradiol in blood. Estrogen raises it, androgens and obesity lower it, changing free hormone levels.
Loss or abnormal distribution of body fat. Can be seen with HIV protease inhibitors and causes insulin resistance.
Blood tests of liver injury and function: AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin and INR.
Surgical removal of a testicle, done for testicular cancer or androgen deprivation in prostate cancer.
A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that blocks conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone. Treats benign prostatic hyperplasia and male pattern baldness.
New-onset high blood pressure after 20 weeks of pregnancy without proteinuria or organ damage. Resolves postpartum but may progress to preeclampsia.
An aggressive breast cancer where tumor emboli block dermal lymphatics, giving red, swollen skin with peau d'orange. Often no discrete mass.
Proliferation of dyscohesive cells within breast lobules, from E-cadherin loss. Often multifocal and bilateral, and a marker of raised risk for invasive cancer.
The inner fetal membrane enclosing the amniotic fluid. Derived from epiblast.
A potassium-sparing diuretic blocking ENaC sodium channels in the collecting duct. Causes hyperkalemia; used for lithium-induced diabetes insipidus.
Brainstem neurons controlling breathing: the medullary dorsal and ventral respiratory groups, and the pontine pneumotaxic and apneustic centers.
The most abundant phospholipid in cell membranes and the main component of lung surfactant (as dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine) and bile.
Abnormal proliferation of placental trophoblast, including hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma. Causes very high hCG.
A purine base pairing with thymine in DNA and uracil in RNA. Part of ATP and cofactors such as NAD and FAD.
A pyrimidine base found in RNA in place of thymine. Pairs with adenine; arises in DNA from cytosine deamination.
Variation in length of short repeated DNA sequences due to defective mismatch repair. Seen in Lynch syndrome and some sporadic colon cancers.
A rifamycin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase. Used for Mycobacterium avium complex and TB in HIV, as it induces CYP450 less than rifampin.
An enzyme that attaches the correct amino acid to its tRNA using ATP. Proofreading ensures accurate translation.
Toxins of Shigella dysenteriae and enterohemorrhagic E. coli that inactivate the 60S ribosome by removing adenine from rRNA. Cause bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
A resting state of the cell cycle in which cells are not dividing. Can be permanent (neurons) or reversible (hepatocytes).
A lysosomal storage disease from failure to add mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes, so they are secreted. Causes coarse facies, skeletal abnormalities and intellectual disability.
Toxin of Clostridium tetani cleaving SNARE protein synaptobrevin in inhibitory neurons, blocking GABA and glycine release. Causes spastic paralysis and lockjaw.
A primary ciliary dyskinesia from dynein arm defects. Presents with situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis and infertility.
A disorder from loss of the maternal UBE3A gene on chromosome 15 (paternal copy silenced). Causes severe intellectual disability, seizures, ataxia and inappropriate laughter.
Mutation in which a three-base sequence repeats excessively. Causes fragile X, Huntington disease and myotonic dystrophy; anticipation occurs.
Specialized cardiac conduction fibers carrying impulses from AV node into the interventricular septum, splitting into right and left bundle branches.
The large vein that returns blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest to the right atrium. Obstruction causes SVC syndrome with facial swelling.
The branch of the common carotid supplying the face and neck, with eight branches including the superior thyroid, lingual, facial, maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
Narrowing of coronary arteries by atherosclerosis, causing angina and myocardial infarction.
Cramping leg pain on walking that is relieved by rest, due to peripheral artery disease. Caused by inadequate muscle blood flow.
A painful ulcerating skin disease with undermined violaceous borders. Associated with inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis and leukemia; shows pathergy.
Any pus-producing bacterial skin infection, such as impetigo or folliculitis.
Severe hypertension with acute end-organ damage such as retinal hemorrhages, papilledema or renal failure. Histology shows hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (onion skinning) and fibrinoid necrosis.
Bleeding in the retina, seen in hypertension, diabetes, retinal vein occlusion and abusive head trauma. Roth spots in endocarditis are an example.
Tissue damage after blood flow returns to ischemic tissue, from oxygen free radicals and calcium overload. Can worsen myocardial infarct size.
The continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee. Susceptible to injury in knee dislocation and to aneurysms.
Drugs ending in -sartan that block AT1 receptors, causing vasodilation. Used in hypertension and heart failure; no cough but are teratogenic.
Receptor for angiotensin II; the AT1 subtype causes vasoconstriction, aldosterone release and sodium retention.
A phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitor raising cAMP, giving positive inotropy and vasodilation. Used short term in acute decompensated heart failure; can cause arrhythmias.
Embryonic heart tissue that forms the atrioventricular septum and valves. Failure to fuse causes atrial and ventricular septal defects, common in Down syndrome.
Early extra heartbeats arising in the ventricles, showing wide QRS complexes. Often benign but may signal underlying heart disease.
Inflammation of the pleura causing sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing and a friction rub.
A lipoprotein protein on chylomicron remnants, VLDL and IDL that lets the liver clear them. The E4 allele increases risk of Alzheimer disease.
Brief neurologic dysfunction from temporary focal brain ischemia without infarction, resolving within 24 hours. A warning sign for stroke.
A drug that blocks the NPC1L1 transporter, reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption. Lowers LDL, usually added to statins.
An antianginal that inhibits the late sodium current, reducing calcium overload without changing heart rate or blood pressure. Can prolong the QT interval.
Muscles of breathing: the diaphragm and external intercostals for inspiration; internal intercostals and abdominal muscles for forced expiration.
The volume of air in the lungs after maximal inspiration. Falls in restrictive lung disease and rises in obstructive disease.

The clear fluid made by the choroid plexus that fills the ventricles and subarachnoid space, cushioning the brain and spinal cord. Sampled by lumbar puncture to diagnose meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
